If I Forget Thee, O Jerusalem
if y for-GET thee oh juh-ROO-suh-lum
n. phr. (the exiles' oath by the rivers of Babylon, Psalm 137:5)
Hebrew 'im-'eshkāchēk y'rūshālaim — the conditional 'im introduces a self-imprecatory oath, the second half of which calls down the penalty: tishkach y'mīnī, let my right hand forget.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Psalm 137 is the Psalter's one song written beside a foreign river. The exiles have hung their harps on the willows, because their captors required of them a song and mirth — sing us one of the songs of Zion — and the psalmist asks how they should sing the LORD's song in a strange land. Then comes the oath: If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning. The oath is doubled in the verse that follows — If I do not remember thee, let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth; if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy. The form is self-imprecation: the singer calls down on himself the loss of the hand that plays and the tongue that sings, the two instruments of the very art his captors are demanding. The oath is not nostalgia for a hometown. Jerusalem was the place of the temple, the ark, the sacrifices and the promise to David, so to forget Jerusalem was to forget the covenant and the God who made it. The refusal to perform the songs of Zion as entertainment, and the vow to prefer that city above his chief joy, are therefore one act of faith: the exile will not let the worship of God be reduced to a captor's amusement, and will not let distance make him forget.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Forget, to lose the remembrance of. Cunning, knowledge; skill; dexterity in performance. Psalm 137:5, the exile's self-imprecatory oath.

expand to see more

Forget, to lose the remembrance of; to let go from the memory.

Cunning, knowledge; art; skill; dexterity in the performance of a thing.

Captivity, the state of being a prisoner, or of being in the power of an enemy.

Hebrew shākach, to forget, cease to care for, ignore.

Hebrew dābaq, to cleave or cling — the tongue to the roof of the mouth. Psalm 137:6.

Key Scripture

Psa 137:1 — "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion."

Psa 137:4 — "How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?"

Psa 137:5 — "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning."

Psa 137:6 — "If I do not remember thee, let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth; if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy."

Modern Corruption

The oath is read as mere patriotism or ethnic sentiment, and the psalm as a whole is dismissed for its closing imprecation rather than handled as inspired Scripture.

expand to see more

Reduced to homesickness, the verse becomes a model for loving one's country and nothing more. The singer's subject is not a landscape but a covenant: Jerusalem held the house where God had put His name, and the songs the captors wanted were the songs of Zion, worship wrenched out of its setting and sold as entertainment. The modern parallel is exact enough to be uncomfortable — sacred song performed for an audience that wants the sound and not the God — and the psalmist's answer is to hang up the harp rather than oblige.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover concerns the psalm's ending, which is now the reason it is most often skipped: the blessing pronounced on him that dasheth the little ones against the stones. It is an imprecation, it is inspired, and it is a prayer that God will do what He had already declared through Isaiah that He would do to Babylon. It is not a licence for private vengeance — the psalmist asks God to act and does not act himself — and it belongs to the same Scripture that forbids the believer to avenge himself. An editor who keeps verses one to six and drops the rest has decided he is a better judge than the Spirit who gave the whole.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'im, introducing a self-imprecatory oath — the hand and tongue forfeited if Jerusalem, and so the covenant, is forgotten.

expand to see more

Hebrew shākach, to forget or cease to care for.

The particle 'im opens a conditional self-curse, with the penalty named after.

Hebrew dābaq, to cleave; the tongue to the palate, Psalm 137:6.

The forfeits are the harpist's hand and the singer's tongue — the captors' demand.

Jerusalem stands for the temple, the covenant and the promise to David.

Usage

"if I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning"

"how shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?"

"if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy"
